e-12442.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of a Line Given a Point and Direction Vector
e-12442.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(3,-1,7)$ and parallel to $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$
e-12442.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $\mathbf{v}$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{v},
$$

where $t \in (-\infty, \infty)$ and $\mathbf{p}$ is the position vector of $P$.

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

e-12443.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
e-12443.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $P(1,-1,2)$ and $Q(3,2,7).$
e-12443.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $\mathbf{v}$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{v},
$$

where $t \in (-\infty, \infty)$ and $\mathbf{p}$ is the position vector of $P.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $P(1,-1,2)$ and $Q(3,2,7),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =⟨3,2,7⟩-⟨1,-1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨2,3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

e-12444.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
e-12444.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(1,2,0)$ and parallel to $\mathbf{v}= \langle -4,1,1 \rangle.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $PA=6\sqrt{2}.$
e-12444.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨1,2,0⟩+t⟨-4,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t \in (-\infty, \infty).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\overrightarrow{OA} = \langle 1, 2, 0 \rangle + t \langle -4, 1, 1 \rangle
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨1,2,0⟩+t⟨-4,1,1⟩)-⟨1,2,0⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-4,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-4t,\,t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=6\sqrt{2},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}PA & =6\sqrt{2} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =6\sqrt{2} \\ |⟨-4t,\,t,\,t⟩| & =6\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{(-4t)^{2}+{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =6\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{18{t}^{2}} & =6\sqrt{2} \\ \pm 3t\sqrt{2} & =6\sqrt{2} \\ t & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 2$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨1,2,0⟩+2⟨-4,1,1⟩=⟨-7,4,2⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨1,2,0⟩-2⟨-4,1,1⟩=⟨9,0,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are $A_1(-7, 4, 2)$ and $A_2(9, 0, -2).$

e-12445.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Segment
e-12445.problem: Using $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}$ notation, find a parametrization of the line segment $\overline{PQ},$ where $P(-4,1,2)$ and $Q(-2,5,-1).$
e-12445.worked_solution:
We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(-2\,i+5\,j-k)-(-4\,i+j+2\,k) \\  & =2\,i+4\,j-3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{v} 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{r} = (-4 \, \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 2\,\mathbf{k}) + t (2 \, \mathbf{i} + 4 \, \mathbf{j} - 3 \, \mathbf{k})
$$

and the parametrization of the line segment $\overline{PQ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(-4\,i+j+2\,k)+t(2\,i+4\,j-3\,k) \\  & =(2t-4)\,i+(4t+1)\,j+(2-3t)\,k,\,t\in [0,1].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through Q(3,112,−7) and parallel to v=⟨1,1,−2⟩.

a
r=⟨1,1,−2⟩+⟨−7,112,3⟩
b
r=⟨112,3,−7⟩+t⟨−1,1,−2⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=⟨1,1,−2⟩+t⟨−7,112,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=⟨1,1,−2⟩+t⟨3,112,−7⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=⟨3,112,−7⟩+t⟨1,1,−2⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit

decision.explanation: A line through Q with direction vector v has equation r=Q+tv. Substituting Q=(√3,11/2,-7) and v=⟨1,1,-2⟩ gives option e.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q(\sqrt{3},\,\frac{11}{2},\,-7)$ and parallel to $v=⟨1,\,1,\,-2⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=q+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$ 

In our case, the position vector of the point $Q$ is $q=⟨\sqrt{3},\,\frac{11}{2},\,-7⟩.$ 

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
r=⟨\sqrt{3},\,\frac{11}{2},\,-7⟩+t⟨1,\,1,\,-2⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through Q(3,112,−7) and parallel to v=⟨1,1,−2⟩.

a
r=⟨1,1,−2⟩+⟨−7,112,3⟩
b
r=⟨112,3,−7⟩+t⟨−1,1,−2⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=⟨1,1,−2⟩+t⟨−7,112,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=⟨1,1,−2⟩+t⟨3,112,−7⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=⟨3,112,−7⟩+t⟨1,1,−2⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through Q and parallel to v is given by r=q+tv,

where t∈(−∞,∞) and q is the position vector of Q.

In our case, the position vector of the point Q is q=⟨3,112,−7⟩.

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

r=⟨3,112,−7⟩+t⟨1,1,−2⟩,t∈(−∞,∞).

Question 2
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through P(−2,1,8) and parallel to v=⟨8,0,−5⟩.

a
r=⟨8,0,−5⟩+t⟨1,−2,8⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=⟨−2,1,8⟩+⟨8,0,−5⟩
c
r=⟨8,0,−5⟩+t⟨−2,1,8⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=⟨−2,1,8⟩+t⟨8,0,−5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=⟨1,8,−2⟩+t⟨8,−5,0⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit

decision.explanation: Use r=p+tv, where p is the position vector of P and v is the direction vector. Thus r=⟨-2,1,8⟩+t⟨8,0,-5⟩ for all real t, which is option d.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(-2,1,8)$ and parallel to $v=⟨8,0,-5⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $p=⟨-2,1,8⟩.$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨-2,1,8⟩+t⟨8,0,-5⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through P(−2,1,8) and parallel to v=⟨8,0,−5⟩.

a
r=⟨8,0,−5⟩+t⟨1,−2,8⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=⟨−2,1,8⟩+⟨8,0,−5⟩
c
r=⟨8,0,−5⟩+t⟨−2,1,8⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=⟨−2,1,8⟩+t⟨8,0,−5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=⟨1,8,−2⟩+t⟨8,−5,0⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through P and parallel to v is given by r=p+tv,

where t∈(−∞,∞) and p is the position vector of P.

In our case, the position vector of the point P is p=⟨−2,1,8⟩.

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

r=⟨−2,1,8⟩+t⟨8,0,−5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞).

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option d: r=p+tv with p=⟨-2,1,8⟩ and v=⟨8,0,-5⟩. At t=0 the line passes through P, and its direction is v.

content.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(-2,1,8)$ and parallel to $v=⟨8,0,-5⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $p=⟨-2,1,8⟩.$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨-2,1,8⟩+t⟨8,0,-5⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

b

c
r=⟨3,−3,3⟩+t⟨23,3,−5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=⟨−3,3,3⟩+t⟨23,−5,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)

Submit

decision.explanation: Use r=q+tv, with q=⟨-3,3,3⟩ and v=⟨√2/3,-5,3⟩. This gives option d; t=0 gives Q and the direction vector is v.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q(-3,3,3)$ and parallel to $v=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-5,3⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=q+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $Q$ is $q=⟨-3,3,3⟩.$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨-3,3,3⟩+t⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-5,3⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through Q(−3,3,3) and parallel to v=⟨23,−5,3⟩.

a
r=⟨−5,3,23⟩+t⟨3,3,−3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=⟨−3,3,3⟩+⟨23,−5,3⟩
c
r=⟨3,−3,3⟩+t⟨23,3,−5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=⟨−3,3,3⟩+t⟨23,−5,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=⟨23,−5,3⟩+t⟨−3,3,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through Q and parallel to v is given by r=q+tv,

where t∈(−∞,∞) and q is the position vector of Q.

In our case, the position vector of the point Q is q=⟨−3,3,3⟩.

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

r=⟨−3,3,3⟩+t⟨23,−5,3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞).

content.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q(-3,3,3)$ and parallel to $v=⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-5,3⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=q+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $Q$ is $q=⟨-3,3,3⟩.$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨-3,3,3⟩+t⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-5,3⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The line has equation r=p+tv. Using p=⟨3,-2,5⟩ and v=⟨4,1,6⟩ gives option b.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(3,-2,5)$ and parallel to $v=⟨4,1,6⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $p=⟨3,-2,5⟩.$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨3,-2,5⟩+t⟨4,1,6⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through P(3,−2,5) and parallel to v=⟨4,1,6⟩.

a
r=⟨6,4,1⟩+t⟨3,−2,5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=⟨3,−2,5⟩+t⟨4,1,6⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=⟨5,−2,3⟩+t⟨6,4,1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=⟨4,1,6⟩+⟨3,−2,5⟩
e
r=⟨4,1,6⟩+t⟨3,−2,5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through P and parallel to v is given by r=p+tv,

where t∈(−∞,∞) and p is the position vector of P.

In our case, the position vector of the point P is p=⟨3,−2,5⟩.

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

r=⟨3,−2,5⟩+t⟨4,1,6⟩,t∈(−∞,∞).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option b. The equation r=p+tv starts at P=(3,-2,5) when t=0 and has direction ⟨4,1,6⟩. Option d has no parameter and represents only one point.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of a Line Given a Point and Direction Vector
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(3,-2,5)$ and parallel to $v=⟨4,1,6⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $p=⟨3,-2,5⟩.$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨3,-2,5⟩+t⟨4,1,6⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(1,-\sqrt{2},-3)$ and parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 9 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $p=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\sqrt{2} \\ -3\end{aligned}].$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\sqrt{2} \\ -3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 9 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through P(1,−2,−3) and parallel to v=[−593].

a
r=[−593]+t[1−2−3],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[−3−21]+t[93−5],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[−593]+t[−2−31],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[1−2−3]+t[−593],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=[1−2−3]+[−593]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through P and parallel to v is given by r=p+tv,

where t∈(−∞,∞) and p is the position vector of P.

In our case, the position vector of the point P is p=[1−2−3].

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

r=[1−2−3]+t[−593],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of a Line Given a Point and Direction Vector
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the straight line passing through $P(1,-\sqrt{2},-3)$ and parallel to $v=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 9 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $P$ is $p=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\sqrt{2} \\ -3\end{aligned}].$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\sqrt{2} \\ -3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 9 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points P(0,−2,−4) and Q(5,0,1).

a
r=[0−2−4]+t[501],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[501]+t[5−25],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[501]+t[0−2−4],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[0−2−4]+t[525],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=[0−2−4]+t[5−25],t∈(−∞,∞)

decision.explanation: The direction vector is Q−P=(5,2,5). Therefore r=P+t(Q−P), which is option d and reaches Q when t=1.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $P(0,-2,-4)$ and $Q(5,0,1).$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $P(0,-2,-4)$ and $Q(5,0,1)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =⟨5,0,1⟩-⟨0,-2,-4⟩ \\  & =⟨5,2,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points P(0,−2,−4) and Q(5,0,1).

a
r=[0−2−4]+t[501],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[501]+t[5−25],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[501]+t[0−2−4],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=[0−2−4]+t[525],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=[0−2−4]+t[5−25],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through P and parallel to v is given by r=p+tv, where t∈(−∞,∞) and p is the position vector of P.

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points P(0,−2,−4) and Q(5,0,1), as follows:

v=PQ→=⟨5,0,1⟩−⟨0,−2,−4⟩=⟨5,2,5⟩

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

r=[0−2−4]+t[525],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $P(0,-2,-4)$ and $Q(5,0,1).$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $P(0,-2,-4)$ and $Q(5,0,1)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =⟨5,0,1⟩-⟨0,-2,-4⟩ \\  & =⟨5,2,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

a
 r=[33−1]+t[35−1],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
r=[010]+t[33−1],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
 r=[34−1]+t[2−2−3],t∈(−∞,∞)

decision.explanation: The direction vector is N−M=(3,3,-1). Using r=M+t(N−M) gives option b, with M at t=0 and N at t=1.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $M(0,1,0)$ and $N(3,4,-1).$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $M$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=m+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $m$ is the position vector of $M.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $M(0,1,0)$ and $N(3,4,-1)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{MN} \\  & =⟨3,4,-1⟩-⟨0,1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨3,3,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $M(0,1,0)$ and $N(3,4,-1).$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $M$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=m+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $m$ is the position vector of $M.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $M(0,1,0)$ and $N(3,4,-1)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{MN} \\  & =⟨3,4,-1⟩-⟨0,1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨3,3,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The direction vector is L−K=(1−(-4),2−(-3),4−(-1))=(5,5,5). Thus r=K+t(5,5,5), which is option b.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $K(-4,-3,-1)$ and $L(1,2,4).$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $K$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=k+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $k$ is the position vector of $K.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $K(-4,-3,-1)$ and $L(1,2,4),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{KL} \\  & =⟨1,2,4⟩-⟨-4,-3,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨5,5,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through K and parallel to v is given by r=k+tv, where t∈(−∞,∞) and k is the position vector of K.

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points K(−4,−3,−1) and L(1,2,4), as follows:

v=KL→=⟨1,2,4⟩−⟨−4,−3,−1⟩=⟨5,5,5⟩

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by r=[−4−3−1]+t[555],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $K(-4,-3,-1)$ and $L(1,2,4).$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $K$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=k+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $k$ is the position vector of $K.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $K(-4,-3,-1)$ and $L(1,2,4),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{KL} \\  & =⟨1,2,4⟩-⟨-4,-3,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨5,5,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

a

b

c

decision.explanation: The direction vector is Q−P=(4,-6,-2). Therefore r=P+t(Q−P), giving option e. At t=0 the line passes through P, and at t=1 it passes through Q.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $P(-1,5,4)$ and $Q(3,-1,2).$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $P(-1,5,4)$ and $Q(3,-1,2)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =⟨3,-1,2⟩-⟨-1,5,4⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-6,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -6 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

a
 r=[3−12]+t[246],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
 r=[−154]+t[3−12],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
 r=[3−12]+t[2−24],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
 r=[4−6−2]+t[−154],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=[−154]+t[4−6−2],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The vector equation of the straight line passing through P and parallel to v is given by r=p+tv, where t∈(−∞,∞) and p is the position vector of P.

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points P(−1,5,4) and Q(3,−1,2), as follows:

v=PQ→=⟨3,−1,2⟩−⟨−1,5,4⟩=⟨4,−6,−2⟩

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

r=[−154]+t[4−6−2],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Vector Equation of the Line Passing Through Two Given Points
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $P(-1,5,4)$ and $Q(3,-1,2).$
content.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $P(-1,5,4)$ and $Q(3,-1,2)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =⟨3,-1,2⟩-⟨-1,5,4⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-6,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -6 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points C(−1,0,4) and D(−7,2,11).

a
 r=[−104]+t[62−7],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
 r=[40−1]+t[−627],t∈(−∞,∞)
c
r=[−104]+t[−627],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
 r=[−104]+t[2−67],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
 r=[10−4]+t[−627],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit

decision.explanation: The direction vector is D−C=(-7−(-1),2−0,11−4)=(-6,2,7). Therefore r=C+t(D−C), which is option c.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the line that passes through the points $C(-1,0,4)$ and $D(-7,2,11).$
after.worked_solution:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $C$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=c+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $c$ is the position vector of $C.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $C(-1,0,4)$ and $D(-7,2,11)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{CD} \\  & =⟨-7,2,11⟩-⟨-1,0,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-6,2,7⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(4,0,-1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,-6,3⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $PA=7.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨4,0,-1⟩+t⟨2,-6,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨4,0,-1⟩+t⟨2,-6,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨4,0,-1⟩+t⟨2,-6,3⟩)-⟨4,0,-1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨2,-6,3⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,-6t,\,3t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=7,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}PA & =7 \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =7 \\ |⟨2t,\,-6t,\,3t⟩| & =7 \\ \sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(-6t)^{2}+(3t)^{2}} & =7 \\ \sqrt{49{t}^{2}} & =7 \\ \pm 7t & =7 \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨4,0,-1⟩+⟨2,-6,3⟩=⟨6,-6,2⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨4,0,-1⟩-⟨2,-6,3⟩=⟨2,6,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(6,-6,2)$ and ${A}_{2}(2,6,-4).$

Question 11
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(4,0,−1) and is parallel to v=⟨2,−6,3⟩. Find all the possible points A on that line such that PA=7.

a
A1(10,2,2) and A2(2,6,−4)
b
A1(6,−6,2) and A2(10,18,8)
c
A1(10,2,2) and A2(7,6,−3)
d
A1(8,−12,5) and A2(7,6,−3)
e
A1(6,−6,2) and A2(2,6,−4)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

r=p+tvr=⟨4,0,−1⟩+t⟨2,−6,3⟩

where t∈(−∞,∞).

Since A lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number t such that

OA→=⟨4,0,−1⟩+t⟨2,−6,3⟩

and

PA→=OA→−OP→=(⟨4,0,−1⟩+t⟨2,−6,3⟩)−⟨4,0,−1⟩=t⟨2,−6,3⟩=⟨2t,−6t,3t⟩.

Using the fact that PA=7, we get:

PA=7|PA→|=7|⟨2t,−6t,3t⟩|=7(2t)2+(−6t)2+(3t)2=749t2=7±7t=7t=±1

Finally, putting the values t=±1 into the equation for the line, we obtain OA1→=⟨4,0,−1⟩+⟨2,−6,3⟩=⟨6,−6,2⟩,OA2→=⟨4,0,−1⟩−⟨2,−6,3⟩=⟨2,6,−4⟩.

Therefore, the points are A1(6,−6,2) and A2(2,6,−4).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
content.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(4,0,-1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,-6,3⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $PA=7.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨4,0,-1⟩+t⟨2,-6,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨4,0,-1⟩+t⟨2,-6,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨4,0,-1⟩+t⟨2,-6,3⟩)-⟨4,0,-1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨2,-6,3⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,-6t,\,3t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=7,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}PA & =7 \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =7 \\ |⟨2t,\,-6t,\,3t⟩| & =7 \\ \sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(-6t)^{2}+(3t)^{2}} & =7 \\ \sqrt{49{t}^{2}} & =7 \\ \pm 7t & =7 \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨4,0,-1⟩+⟨2,-6,3⟩=⟨6,-6,2⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨4,0,-1⟩-⟨2,-6,3⟩=⟨2,6,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(6,-6,2)$ and ${A}_{2}(2,6,-4).$

Consider the straight line that passes through P(1,1,1) and is parallel to v=⟨1,−1,5⟩. Find all the possible points Q on that line such that PQ=33.

a
Q1(3,−1,11) and Q2(0,2,−4)
b
Q1(2,0,6) and Q2(0,2,−4)
c
Q1(6,2,2) and Q2(1,0,−2)
d
Q1(4,2,6) and Q2(1,0,2)
e
Q1(2,0,6) and Q2(−1,3,−9)
Submit

decision.explanation: Write Q=P+tv. Since |v|=√(1+1+25)=3√3, the distance condition gives |t|=1. Thus Q=P±v yields (2,0,6) and (0,2,-4), option b.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(1,1,1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨1,-1,5⟩.$ Find all the possible points $Q$ on that line such that $PQ=3\sqrt{3}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $Q$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OQ} & =⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩)-⟨1,1,1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨1,-1,5⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,-t,\,5t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PQ=3\sqrt{3},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}PQ & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |\overset{\to }{PQ}| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |⟨t,\,-t,\,5t⟩| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+(-t)^{2}+(5t)^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{27{t}^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \pm 3\sqrt{3}t & =3\sqrt{3} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{Q}_{1}}=⟨1,1,1⟩+⟨1,-1,5⟩=⟨2,0,6⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{Q}_{2}}=⟨1,1,1⟩-⟨1,-1,5⟩=⟨0,2,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${Q}_{1}(2,0,6)$ and ${Q}_{2}(0,2,-4).$

Question 12
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(1,1,1) and is parallel to v=⟨1,−1,5⟩. Find all the possible points Q on that line such that PQ=33.

a
Q1(3,−1,11) and Q2(0,2,−4)
b
Q1(2,0,6) and Q2(0,2,−4)
c
Q1(6,2,2) and Q2(1,0,−2)
d
Q1(4,2,6) and Q2(1,0,2)
e
Q1(2,0,6) and Q2(−1,3,−9)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

r=p+tvr=⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,−1,5⟩ where t∈(−∞,∞).

Since Q lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number t such that

OQ→=⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,−1,5⟩

and

PQ→=OQ→−OP→=(⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,−1,5⟩)−⟨1,1,1⟩=t⟨1,−1,5⟩=⟨t,−t,5t⟩.

Using the fact that PQ=33, we get:

PQ=33|PQ→|=33|⟨t,−t,5t⟩|=33t2+(−t)2+(5t)2=3327t2=33±33t=33t=±1

Finally, putting the values t=±1 into the equation for the line, we obtain

OQ1→=⟨1,1,1⟩+⟨1,−1,5⟩=⟨2,0,6⟩,OQ2→=⟨1,1,1⟩−⟨1,−1,5⟩=⟨0,2,−4⟩. Therefore, the points are Q1(2,0,6) and Q2(0,2,−4).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option b. Since |v|=√27=3√3, the distance condition |t||v|=3√3 gives t=±1. Therefore Q=P±v gives (2,0,6) and (0,2,-4).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
content.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(1,1,1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨1,-1,5⟩.$ Find all the possible points $Q$ on that line such that $PQ=3\sqrt{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $Q$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OQ} & =⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨1,1,1⟩+t⟨1,-1,5⟩)-⟨1,1,1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨1,-1,5⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,-t,\,5t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PQ=3\sqrt{3},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}PQ & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |\overset{\to }{PQ}| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ |⟨t,\,-t,\,5t⟩| & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+(-t)^{2}+(5t)^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{27{t}^{2}} & =3\sqrt{3} \\ \pm 3\sqrt{3}t & =3\sqrt{3} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{Q}_{1}}=⟨1,1,1⟩+⟨1,-1,5⟩=⟨2,0,6⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{Q}_{2}}=⟨1,1,1⟩-⟨1,-1,5⟩=⟨0,2,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${Q}_{1}(2,0,6)$ and ${Q}_{2}(0,2,-4).$

Question 13
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(3,−2,3) and is parallel to v=⟨−2,1,2⟩. Find all the possible points A on that line such that AP=3.

a
A1(1,−1,5) and A2(5,−3,1)
b
A1(1,2,5) and A2(−5,3,1)
c
A1(1,1,−5) and A2(5,3,2)
d
A1(1,−1,−5) and A2(5,3,2)
e
A1(−1,−1,5) and A2(4,−3,−1)
Submit

decision.explanation: Write A=P+tv. Since |v|=√(4+1+4)=3, AP=3|t|=3 gives t=±1. Thus P±v gives (1,-1,5) and (5,-3,1), option a.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(3,-2,3)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨-2,1,2⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=3.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩)-⟨3,-2,3⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-2,1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,\,t,\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=3,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =3 \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =3 \\ |⟨-2t,\,t,\,2t⟩| & =3 \\ \sqrt{(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} & =3 \\ \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} & =3 \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}} & =3 \\ \pm 3t & =3 \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨3,-2,3⟩+⟨-2,1,2⟩=⟨1,-1,5⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨3,-2,3⟩-⟨-2,1,2⟩=⟨5,-3,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(1,-1,5)$ and ${A}_{2}(5,-3,1).$

Question 13
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(3,−2,3) and is parallel to v=⟨−2,1,2⟩. Find all the possible points A on that line such that AP=3.

a
A1(1,−1,5) and A2(5,−3,1)
b
A1(1,2,5) and A2(−5,3,1)
c
A1(1,1,−5) and A2(5,3,2)
d
A1(1,−1,−5) and A2(5,3,2)
e
A1(−1,−1,5) and A2(4,−3,−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

r=p+tvr=⟨3,−2,3⟩+t⟨−2,1,2⟩ where t∈(−∞,∞).

Since A lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number t such that

OA→=⟨3,−2,3⟩+t⟨−2,1,2⟩

and

PA→=OA→−OP→=(⟨3,−2,3⟩+t⟨−2,1,2⟩)−⟨3,−2,3⟩=t⟨−2,1,2⟩=⟨−2t,t,2t⟩.

Using the fact that PA=3, we get:

AP=3|PA→|=3|⟨−2t,t,2t⟩|=3(−2t)2+t2+(2t)2=34t2+t2+4t2=39t2=3±3t=3t=±1

Finally, putting the values t=±1 into the equation for the line, we obtain

OA1→=⟨3,−2,3⟩+⟨−2,1,2⟩=⟨1,−1,5⟩,OA2→=⟨3,−2,3⟩−⟨−2,1,2⟩=⟨5,−3,1⟩. Therefore, the points are A1(1,−1,5) and A2(5,−3,1).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
content.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(3,-2,3)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨-2,1,2⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=3.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨3,-2,3⟩+t⟨-2,1,2⟩)-⟨3,-2,3⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-2,1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2t,\,t,\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=3,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =3 \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =3 \\ |⟨-2t,\,t,\,2t⟩| & =3 \\ \sqrt{(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} & =3 \\ \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} & =3 \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}} & =3 \\ \pm 3t & =3 \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨3,-2,3⟩+⟨-2,1,2⟩=⟨1,-1,5⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨3,-2,3⟩-⟨-2,1,2⟩=⟨5,-3,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(1,-1,5)$ and ${A}_{2}(5,-3,1).$

OA1→=⟨3,−2,3⟩+⟨−2,1,2⟩=⟨1,−1,5⟩,OA2→=⟨3,−2,3⟩−⟨−2,1,2⟩=⟨5,−3,1⟩. Therefore, the points are A1(1,−1,5) and A2(5,−3,1).

Question 14
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(2,3,6) and is parallel to v=⟨−3,−2,1⟩. Find all the possible points A on that line such that AP=14.

a
A1(−1,1,−7) and A2(5,5,5)
b
A1(−1,1,7) and A2(5,5,5)
c
A1(1,−1,−7) and A2(5,5,5)
d
A1(−1,−1,7) and A2(5,−5,5)
e
A1(1,1,7) and A2(5,−5,5)
Submit

decision.explanation: Points on the line satisfy A=P+tv. Since |v|=√(9+4+1)=√14, the required distance gives |t|=1. Thus P+v=(-1,1,7) and P−v=(5,5,5), matching option b.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(2,3,6)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨-3,-2,1⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=\sqrt{14}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩)-⟨2,3,6⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-3,-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{14},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{14} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{14} \\ |⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩| & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{(-3t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \pm t\sqrt{14} & =\sqrt{14} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨2,3,6⟩+⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨-1,1,7⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨2,3,6⟩-⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨5,5,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(-1,1,7)$ and ${A}_{2}(5,5,5).$

Question 14
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(2,3,6) and is parallel to v=⟨−3,−2,1⟩. Find all the possible points A on that line such that AP=14.

a
A1(−1,1,−7) and A2(5,5,5)
b
A1(−1,1,7) and A2(5,5,5)
c
A1(1,−1,−7) and A2(5,5,5)
d
A1(−1,−1,7) and A2(5,−5,5)
e
A1(1,1,7) and A2(5,−5,5)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

r=p+tvr=⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨−3,−2,1⟩ where t∈(−∞,∞).

Since A lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number t such that

OA→=⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨−3,−2,1⟩

and

PA→=OA→−OP→=(⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨−3,−2,1⟩)−⟨2,3,6⟩=t⟨−3,−2,1⟩=⟨−3t,−2t,t⟩.

Using the fact that PA=14, we get:

AP=14|PA→|=14|⟨−3t,−2t,t⟩|=14(−3t)2+(−2t)2+t2=149t2+4t2+t2=14±t14=14t=±1

Finally, putting the values t=±1 into the equation for the line, we obtain

OA1→=⟨2,3,6⟩+⟨−3,−2,1⟩=⟨−1,1,7⟩,OA2→=⟨2,3,6⟩−⟨−3,−2,1⟩=⟨5,5,5⟩. Therefore, the points are A1(−1,1,7) and A2(5,5,5).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
content.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(2,3,6)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨-3,-2,1⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=\sqrt{14}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨2,3,6⟩+t⟨-3,-2,1⟩)-⟨2,3,6⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨-3,-2,1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{14},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{14} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{14} \\ |⟨-3t,\,-2t,\,t⟩| & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{(-3t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \pm t\sqrt{14} & =\sqrt{14} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨2,3,6⟩+⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨-1,1,7⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨2,3,6⟩-⟨-3,-2,1⟩=⟨5,5,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(-1,1,7)$ and ${A}_{2}(5,5,5).$

OA1→=⟨2,3,6⟩+⟨−3,−2,1⟩=⟨−1,1,7⟩,OA2→=⟨2,3,6⟩−⟨−3,−2,1⟩=⟨5,5,5⟩. Therefore, the points are A1(−1,1,7) and A2(5,5,5).

Your Answer:
A1(−1,1,−7) and A2(5,5,5)

Consider the straight line that passes through P(3,1,−1) and is parallel to v=⟨2,1,3⟩. Find all the possible points A on that line such that AP=14.

a
A1(2,5,2) and A2(0,1,−4)
b
A1(5,2,2) and A2(1,0,−4)
c
A1(4,2,2) and A2(1,0,−4)
d
A1(5,3,2) and A2(1,0,4)
e
A1(5,2,3) and A2(1,−1,−4)
Submit

decision.explanation: Since |v|=√(4+1+9)=√14, A=P+tv has distance AP=|t|√14. Thus t=±1, giving P+v=(5,2,2) and P−v=(1,0,-4), option b.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(3,1,-1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,1,3⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=\sqrt{14}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨3,1,-1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨3,1,-1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨3,1,-1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩)-⟨3,1,-1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨2,1,3⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{14},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{14} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{14} \\ |⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩| & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}+(3t)^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{14{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \pm t\sqrt{14} & =\sqrt{14} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨3,1,-1⟩+1⟨2,1,3⟩=⟨5,2,2⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨3,1,-1⟩-1⟨2,1,3⟩=⟨1,0,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(5,2,2)$ and ${A}_{2}(1,0,-4).$

Question 15
?

Consider the straight line that passes through P(3,1,−1) and is parallel to v=⟨2,1,3⟩. Find all the possible points A on that line such that AP=14.

a
A1(2,5,2) and A2(0,1,−4)
b
A1(5,2,2) and A2(1,0,−4)
c
A1(4,2,2) and A2(1,0,−4)
d
A1(5,3,2) and A2(1,0,4)
e
A1(5,2,3) and A2(1,−1,−4)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

r=p+tvr=⟨3,1,−1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩ where t∈(−∞,∞).

Since A lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number t such that

OA→=⟨3,1,−1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩

and

PA→=OA→−OP→=(⟨3,1,−1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩)−⟨3,1,−1⟩=t⟨2,1,3⟩=⟨2t,t,3t⟩.

Using the fact that PA=14, we get:

AP=14|PA→|=14|⟨2t,t,3t⟩|=14(2t)2+t2+(3t)2=1414t2=14±t14=14t=±1

Finally, putting the values t=±1 into the equation for the line, we obtain

OA1→=⟨3,1,−1⟩+1⟨2,1,3⟩=⟨5,2,2⟩,OA2→=⟨3,1,−1⟩−1⟨2,1,3⟩=⟨1,0,−4⟩. Therefore, the points are A1(5,2,2) and A2(1,0,−4).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points on a Line That Are a Fixed Distance From Another Point on the Line
content.problem: Consider the straight line that passes through $P(3,1,-1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,1,3⟩.$ Find all the possible points $A$ on that line such that $AP=\sqrt{14}.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨3,1,-1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨3,1,-1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨3,1,-1⟩+t⟨2,1,3⟩)-⟨3,1,-1⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨2,1,3⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{14},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{14} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{14} \\ |⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩| & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{t}^{2}+(3t)^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \sqrt{14{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{14} \\ \pm t\sqrt{14} & =\sqrt{14} \\ t & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 1$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨3,1,-1⟩+1⟨2,1,3⟩=⟨5,2,2⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨3,1,-1⟩-1⟨2,1,3⟩=⟨1,0,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${A}_{1}(5,2,2)$ and ${A}_{2}(1,0,-4).$

before.problem:
The equation below describes all the points on the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ},$ where $P(-6,2,-1)$ and $Q(-8,0,-1).$

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ a\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ b \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,c]

$$

$$

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,1].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Segment
content.problem:
The equation below gives a parametrization of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ},$ where $P(3,2,-1)$ and $Q(0,1,-3).$

$$
r(t)=a\,i+b\,j-(2t+1)\,k,\,t\in [0,c]
$$

What is $a+b+c?$
content.worked_solution:
We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(j-3\,k)-(3\,i+2\,j-k) \\  & =-3\,i-j-2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
r=p+tv\,⟹\,r=(3\,i+2\,j-k)+t(-3\,i-j-2\,k)
$$

and the parametrization of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(3\,i+2\,j-k)+t(-3\,i-j-2\,k) \\  & =(3-3t)\,i+(2-t)\,j-(2t+1)\,k,\,t\in [0,1].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=(3-3t)+(2-t)+1=6-4t.
$$
